title: Establish AI Governance, Frameworks, and Policies
intro: The laws, frameworks and standards that shape AI governance (the EU AI Act, GDPR, the NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001), what makes governing AI different from governing IT, the policy stack that turns intent into action, the centralised AI use-case inventory, and the roles that make governance work.
objectives: Explain the EU AI Act’s risk tiers, roles, key obligations and timeline, and how GDPR applies to AI
Describe the NIST AI RMF functions and trustworthy characteristics, and the structure of ISO/IEC 42001
Explain how AI governance extends traditional IT governance

sections.title: The legal landscape: the EU AI Act and GDPR

scenes.title: The rulebook for AI
scenes.sub: The EU AI Act, GDPR, and why they reach far beyond Europe
scenes.say: Before an organisation can govern AI, it needs to know which rules apply. | This video introduces the two laws you are most likely to meet: the EU AI Act and the GDPR, and explains how they differ from frameworks and standards.

scenes.title: Laws, frameworks and standards
scenes.say: Governance draws on three kinds of source. | Laws, such as the EU AI Act and the GDPR, are binding and enforced with fines. Frameworks, such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, are voluntary guidance. Standards, such as ISO/IEC 42001, are voluntary, but some can be certified by an independent auditor. | Laws set legal duties. Frameworks give you a structured way to manage risk. Management system standards define a system that an auditor can check. | And each produces different evidence: records and registrations for regulators, documented profiles for frameworks, and audit reports for certification.

scenes.title: The EU AI Act’s risk tiers

layers.label: Unacceptable risk: prohibited
layers.sub: Social scoring, manipulative AI, untargeted facial scraping

layers.label: High risk: strict requirements
layers.sub: Hiring, credit, education, critical infrastructure, safety parts

layers.label: Limited risk: transparency
layers.sub: Chatbots, deepfakes and generated content must be disclosed

layers.label: Minimal risk: no new duties
layers.sub: Spam filters, game AI, most everyday tools

scenes.say: The EU AI Act regulates AI by risk, in four tiers. | At the top are unacceptable practices, which are banned outright, such as social scoring and untargeted scraping of facial images. | Next come high-risk systems, used in areas like hiring, credit, education, critical infrastructure and product safety. These carry strict requirements. | Limited-risk systems carry transparency duties: people must know when they are talking to a chatbot, and deepfakes and generated content must be disclosed. | Everything else is minimal risk, with no new obligations. Separately, the Act sets duties for providers of general-purpose AI models, with extra duties for the most capable ones.

scenes.title: Banned outright (Article 5)

items.d: Subliminal or deceptive techniques; exploiting age or disability
Rating people on behaviour, leading to unfair treatment
Predicting offences from personality traits alone
Building face databases from the web or CCTV
At work or school, except for medical or safety reasons
Inferring race or beliefs; real-time police identification

scenes.say: Article five lists the banned practices. They have applied since February twenty twenty-five. | Manipulative or deceptive techniques that distort behaviour and cause significant harm, and exploiting people’s vulnerabilities, such as age or disability. | Social scoring that leads to detrimental or unjustified treatment. | Predicting that someone will commit a crime based solely on profiling or personality traits. | Building facial recognition databases by untargeted scraping of images from the internet or CCTV. | Emotion recognition in workplaces and schools, except for medical or safety reasons. | And biometric categorisation to infer sensitive traits such as race or religious beliefs, plus real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement, apart from narrow exceptions.

scenes.title: Providers and deployers
rows: Develops a system and places it on the market under its name
Uses a system under its authority, professionally
Risk management, data governance, documentation, logging, conformity assessment
Use as instructed, human oversight, monitoring, logs, informing people
Duties apply wherever the provider is based
Substantial changes can make you the provider
scenes.say: The Act assigns duties by role. | A provider develops an AI system, or has one developed, and places it on the market under its own name. A deployer uses an AI system under its authority in a professional capacity. | Providers of high-risk systems carry most of the burden: risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, conformity assessment and post-market monitoring. Deployers must use systems as instructed, assign competent human oversight, monitor operation, keep logs and inform affected people. | Two traps. The Act applies to providers outside the EU when their systems are used in the EU. And a deployer that substantially modifies a high-risk system, or puts its own name on it, becomes its provider.

events.d: Chatbot, deepfake and content marking duties

scenes.say: The obligations phase in over several years, and the 2026 Digital Omnibus amendment moved some dates. | The Act entered into force in August twenty twenty-four. | Prohibitions and the AI literacy duty have applied since February twenty twenty-five. | Duties for general-purpose AI model providers, and the penalty regime, followed in August twenty twenty-five. | Transparency duties for chatbots, deepfakes and generated content have applied since August twenty twenty-six. | High-risk duties for the Annex three use cases, such as hiring and credit, now apply from December twenty twenty-seven. | And high-risk duties for AI built into regulated products follow in August twenty twenty-eight.

scenes.title: GDPR still applies to AI

items.d: Wherever personal data enters training, prompts or outputs
Only what the purpose needs; no silent repurposing
Required when processing is likely to be high risk
Access, erasure, objection; automated-decision safeguards
Protect the data; notify the regulator within 72 hours

scenes.say: The AI Act sits alongside the GDPR, which applies whenever personal data is processed, including inside AI systems. | Every use of personal data needs a lawful basis, whether in training data, fine-tuning, prompts or outputs. | Purpose limitation and data minimisation mean collecting only what the purpose needs, and not quietly reusing data for something new, such as model training. | A data protection impact assessment is required when processing is likely to be high risk, which covers many AI uses. | People keep their rights of access, erasure and objection, and safeguards apply to solely automated decisions with significant effects. | And personal data must be secured, with breaches reported to the regulator within seventy-two hours.

items: Laws bind; frameworks guide; standards can be certified
AI Act: prohibited, high, limited, minimal risk, plus GPAI
Providers carry most duties; deployers have their own
GDPR applies wherever personal data meets AI
scenes.say: To recap. | Laws bind, frameworks guide, and management system standards can be certified. | The EU AI Act sorts AI into prohibited, high-risk, limited-risk and minimal-risk uses, with separate duties for general-purpose models. | Providers carry most obligations, but deployers have their own, and can become providers. | And the GDPR applies wherever personal data meets AI.

blocks.md:
### Why start with law?
Governance is the system of decisions, roles and controls that keeps AI use aligned with an organisation’s objectives, values and legal obligations. Its first job is to know which obligations apply. For most organisations that operate in, sell into or process data from Europe, two laws dominate: the **EU AI Act** and the **General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)**. Both have *extraterritorial* reach, so organisations based elsewhere are often in scope.

### The EU AI Act in brief
The AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, is the first comprehensive horizontal law on AI. It entered into force on 1 August 2024 and applies in phases. It takes a **risk-based approach**:

| Tier | Examples | What applies |
|---|---|---|
| **Prohibited** (Article 5) | Social scoring, manipulative techniques, untargeted facial scraping, workplace emotion recognition | Banned |
| **High risk** (Article 6, Annexes I and III) | Safety components of regulated products; biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, access to essential services such as credit, law enforcement, migration, justice | Strict requirements before and after placing on the market |
| **Limited risk** (Article 50) | Chatbots, emotion recognition, deepfakes, AI-generated content | Transparency duties |
| **Minimal risk** | Spam filters, recommendation of video-game moves | No new obligations; voluntary codes encouraged |

**General-purpose AI (GPAI) models** have their own regime. All GPAI providers must keep technical documentation, give information to downstream providers, maintain a copyright policy and publish a summary of training content. Models with **systemic risk** (presumed above 10²⁵ floating-point operations of training compute) must also perform model evaluations and adversarial testing, assess and mitigate systemic risks, report serious incidents and ensure adequate cybersecurity. A voluntary **GPAI Code of Practice**, published in July 2025, offers a way to demonstrate compliance.

### High-risk requirements
Providers of high-risk systems must implement a **risk management system** (Article 9), **data governance** for training, validation and test data (Article 10), **technical documentation** (Article 11), automatic **logging** (Article 12), **transparency** and instructions for deployers (Article 13), **human oversight** (Article 14), and appropriate **accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity** (Article 15), all under a **quality management system** (Article 17). They complete a **conformity assessment**, affix the CE marking, register in the EU database, run **post-market monitoring** and report **serious incidents**.

**Deployers** (Article 26) must use the system according to its instructions, assign human oversight to competent people, ensure input data is relevant, monitor operation, keep logs for at least six months, and inform workers and affected people. Public bodies and certain private deployers, such as those assessing creditworthiness or pricing life and health insurance, must carry out a **fundamental rights impact assessment** (Article 27), which can build on an existing GDPR DPIA.

Article 15 matters to security professionals: high-risk systems must be resilient against attempts to alter their use or performance by exploiting vulnerabilities, with measures against **data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, confidentiality attacks and model flaws**.

### Penalties
Fines reach up to **€35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover** for prohibited practices, up to €15 million or 3% for most other breaches, and up to €7.5 million or 1% for supplying incorrect information to authorities. Lower ceilings apply to SMEs.

### Timeline after the Digital Omnibus
In 2026 the EU adopted a **Digital Omnibus on AI** (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744), which delayed some deadlines without removing any category of obligation:

- **2 February 2025:** prohibitions and AI literacy (Article 4) apply. The Omnibus softened Article 4 so that organisations must *take measures to support* AI literacy, rather than guarantee a particular level.
- **2 August 2025:** GPAI obligations, governance bodies and penalties apply.
- **2 August 2026:** transparency duties under Article 50 apply. Generative systems already on the market before that date have until **2 December 2026** to add machine-readable marking of their outputs.
- **2 December 2026:** two new prohibitions apply, covering AI that generates non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material.
- **2 December 2027:** high-risk obligations for Annex III use cases (previously August 2026).
- **2 August 2028:** high-risk obligations for AI in products covered by Annex I legislation (previously August 2027).

Exam questions are more likely to test the *structure* (tiers, roles, duties) than exact dates, but you should know the order in which obligations arrive.

### GDPR and AI
The GDPR applies whenever personal data is processed, and AI systems process it at every stage: collected training data, fine-tuning sets, retrieval indexes, prompts, logs and outputs. Its principles (Article 5) are **lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality; and accountability**. Key provisions for AI include:

- **Lawful basis** (Article 6), with stricter conditions for **special category data** such as health, biometrics and religious beliefs (Article 9).
- **Data protection impact assessments** (Article 35) for processing likely to result in high risk, including systematic profiling and new technologies.
- **Rights** of access (including meaningful information about the logic of automated decisions), rectification, erasure and objection, and **Article 22** safeguards for solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects.
- **Data protection by design and by default** (Article 25), **security of processing** (Article 32) and **breach notification** to the supervisory authority within 72 hours (Article 33).
- Restrictions on **international transfers** (Chapter V), relevant when prompts or training data flow to providers in other countries.

In December 2024 the European Data Protection Board published **Opinion 28/2024** on AI models. It said that whether a trained model is anonymous must be assessed case by case (personal data must not be extractable by reasonably likely means), explained how legitimate interest can serve as a lawful basis for developing and deploying models, and warned that unlawful processing during development can affect the lawfulness of later use. GDPR fines reach €20 million or 4% of worldwide turnover.

blocks.title: EU AI Act vocabulary
cards: An organisation that develops an AI system or GPAI model, or has one developed, and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name.
An organisation that uses an AI system under its authority, other than for personal non-professional use.
A system that is a safety component of a regulated product (Annex I), or used in a listed sensitive area such as hiring or credit (Annex III).
The process of showing that a high-risk system meets the Act’s requirements before it is placed on the market.
A highly capable general-purpose model, presumed when training compute exceeds 10²⁵ FLOPs, with extra evaluation, incident and security duties.
An assessment that certain deployers must perform before using high-risk systems, covering impacts on people’s rights.

blocks.title: Role first, then obligations
blocks.md: When a scenario involves the AI Act, first decide the **role** (provider or deployer) and the **tier** (prohibited, high, limited, minimal, or GPAI). The obligations follow from that combination. A company that buys a CV-screening tool is a **deployer of a high-risk system**; if it retrains and rebrands the tool, it may become the **provider**.

blocks.title: The rebranded screening tool
blocks.md: A recruitment firm licenses an AI CV-screening system from a vendor and uses it to shortlist candidates for its clients. To win business, it fine-tunes the model on its own placement data and sells access under its own brand as “TalentLens”.

q.q: How is the recruitment firm MOST likely classified under the EU AI Act?
o: As a deployer only, because the vendor built the original system and remains its provider
As the provider of a high-risk system, because it substantially modified it and markets it under its own name
As outside the Act, because recruitment tools fall into the minimal-risk tier unless they use biometrics
As a general-purpose AI model provider with systemic risk, because it fine-tuned the underlying model
q.why: Employment and recruitment uses are high risk under Annex III. Substantially modifying a high-risk system and placing it on the market under your own name makes you its provider, with the full set of provider obligations.

q.q: Which AI Act tier imposes mainly transparency duties, such as telling people they are interacting with a chatbot?
o: Prohibited
High risk
Limited risk
Minimal risk
q.why: Limited-risk systems, covered by Article 50, carry transparency obligations: disclosing AI interaction and marking or disclosing synthetic content and deepfakes.

sections.title: Frameworks and standards: NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001

scenes.title: Frameworks you can build on
scenes.sub: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001
scenes.say: Laws tell you what outcomes you must achieve. Frameworks and standards help you build the system that achieves them. | This video covers the two you will meet most often: the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and the ISO/IEC 42001 standard for AI management systems.

scenes.title: The NIST AI RMF core
scenes.intro: Voluntary, outcome-based, and usable by any organisation, in any sector.

stages.label: Map
stages.d: Establish context: purpose, users, impacts, and the risks that follow.

stages.label: Measure
stages.d: Assess, test and track risks with suitable metrics.

stages.label: Manage
stages.d: Prioritise and treat risks; respond and recover.

scenes.say: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework, published in January twenty twenty-three, is voluntary and usable by organisations of any size, in any sector. Its core has four functions. | Map establishes context: what the system is for, who uses it and who is affected, and which risks follow. | Measure assesses, tests and tracks those risks with suitable methods and metrics. | Manage prioritises risks, treats them, and responds to and recovers from incidents. | And Govern sits at the centre. It covers culture, policies, roles and accountability, and it runs through every other function.

scenes.title: Seven characteristics of trustworthy AI

items.d: Does what it should, consistently
Doesn’t endanger life, health or property
Withstands attacks and recovers
Clear ownership; information available
Its outputs can be understood
Protects autonomy and personal data
Equitable treatment of people

scenes.say: NIST describes seven characteristics of trustworthy AI. | Valid and reliable: the system does what it is meant to, consistently. This is the foundation for all the others. | Safe: it does not endanger human life, health, property or the environment. | Secure and resilient: it withstands attacks and recovers from them. | Accountable and transparent: ownership is clear, and appropriate information about the system is available. | Explainable and interpretable: people can understand how and why it produced an output. | Privacy-enhanced: it protects people’s autonomy and personal data. | And fair, with harmful bias managed. Note that these characteristics trade off against each other, which is why governance decisions matter.

scenes.title: NIST resources that extend the framework

items.d: Twelve risks that generative AI creates or worsens, with actions
A CSF 2.0 profile: secure AI, defend with AI, thwart AI-enabled attacks
Common language for attacks on predictive and generative AI
SP 800-53 controls tailored to AI use cases

scenes.say: NIST has built a family of resources around the framework. | The Generative AI Profile, NIST AI six hundred dash one, describes twelve risks that generative AI creates or worsens, such as confabulation, information integrity and value-chain risks, with suggested actions for each. | The Cyber AI Profile applies the Cybersecurity Framework two point oh to AI, in three focus areas: securing AI systems, using AI for cyber defence, and thwarting AI-enabled attacks. | The adversarial machine learning taxonomy, NIST AI one hundred dash two, gives a common language for attacks on both predictive and generative AI. | And NIST is developing control overlays that tailor the SP eight hundred dash fifty-three security controls to specific AI use cases.

scenes.title: ISO/IEC 42001: an AI management system
scenes.centerSub: AI management system; certifiable, like ISO/IEC 27001
scenes.intro: Published in 2023, it follows the same harmonised structure as other ISO management system standards.

It uses the same structure as ISO twenty-seven thousand and one, so the two integrate well, and organisations can be certified against it. | Plan covers the organisation’s context, leadership commitment, an AI policy, AI risk assessment, AI system impact assessment and objectives. | Do means operating the controls across the AI life cycle, including data and suppliers. | Check means monitoring and measuring, internal audit, and management review. | And Act means correcting nonconformities and improving continually. Annex A provides thirty-eight reference controls, which the organisation selects and justifies in a statement of applicability.

nodes.label: Laws
nodes.sub: EU AI Act, GDPR, sector rules

Legal obligations are captured in an obligations register. | The register feeds a single AI management system, often built on ISO forty-two thousand and one, which defines the policies, roles and controls. | NIST AI RMF practices strengthen how risks are mapped, measured and managed inside that system. | And because the controls are shared, evidence is collected once and reused for regulators, auditors and customers. Mapping one framework to another is called a crosswalk.

blocks.md:
### The NIST AI Risk Management Framework
The **NIST AI RMF 1.0** (January 2023) is a voluntary, non-sector-specific framework. Part 1 explains how AI risks differ from traditional software risks and defines trustworthy AI. Part 2, the **core**, is organised into four functions, each broken down into categories and subcategories of outcomes:

| Function | Purpose | Examples of outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| **Govern** | Cultivate a risk-aware culture and accountability | Policies and procedures; roles and responsibilities; workforce diversity and training; processes for third-party risk; mechanisms for engaging affected communities |
| **Map** | Establish context and identify risks | Intended purpose and context documented; system categorised; capabilities and limits understood; impacts on individuals and society identified |
| **Measure** | Analyse, assess and track risks | Appropriate metrics selected; systems evaluated for trustworthy characteristics; risks tracked over time; feedback gathered |
| **Manage** | Prioritise and act on risks | Risks prioritised and treated; benefits weighed against costs; third-party risks managed; incidents responded to and communicated |

**Govern** is cross-cutting: it informs and is informed by the other three. The RMF is accompanied by a **Playbook** with suggested actions for each subcategory, and by **profiles** that tailor it to a sector, technology or use case.

The seven **characteristics of trustworthy AI** are: valid and reliable; safe; secure and resilient; accountable and transparent; explainable and interpretable; privacy-enhanced; and fair, with harmful bias managed. *Valid and reliable* is the base on which the others rest, and *accountable and transparent* spans them all. They involve trade-offs: for example, improving privacy by adding noise can reduce accuracy, and the most accurate model may be the least explainable.

**The Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1, July 2024)** lists twelve risks that generative AI creates or exacerbates: CBRN information or capabilities; confabulation; dangerous, violent or hateful content; data privacy; environmental impacts; harmful bias and homogenisation; human–AI configuration; information integrity; information security; intellectual property; obscene, degrading or abusive content; and value chain and component integration.

NIST has also drafted a **Cybersecurity Framework Profile for AI** (the Cyber AI Profile), a CSF 2.0 community profile with three focus areas: *securing* AI system components, *defending* with AI-enabled cybersecurity, and *thwarting* AI-enabled attacks. And it is developing **Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems (COSAiS)**, which tailor SP 800-53 controls to AI use cases such as using and fine-tuning predictive AI.

### ISO/IEC 42001:2023
ISO/IEC 42001 specifies requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving an **AI management system (AIMS)**. It applies to any organisation that provides or uses AI. Like ISO/IEC 27001, it follows the harmonised structure of clauses 4 to 10:

| Clause | Content |
|---|---|
| 4 Context | Internal and external issues, interested parties, scope, the role the organisation plays (for example, provider or user) |
| 5 Leadership | Top-management commitment, AI policy, roles and responsibilities |
| 6 Planning | AI risk assessment and treatment, **AI system impact assessment**, objectives, statement of applicability |
| 7 Support | Resources, competence, awareness, communication, documented information |
| 8 Operation | Operational planning and control; performing risk assessments, treatments and impact assessments |
| 9 Performance evaluation | Monitoring and measurement, internal audit, management review |
| 10 Improvement | Nonconformity, corrective action, continual improvement |

**Annex A** lists 38 reference controls under nine objectives: AI policies; internal organisation; resources for AI systems; assessing impacts of AI systems; the AI system life cycle; data for AI systems; information for interested parties; use of AI systems; and third-party and customer relationships. **Annex B** gives implementation guidance; **Annex C** lists potential organisational objectives and risk sources. The organisation documents which controls it applies, and why, in a **statement of applicability**.

Certification is performed by accredited certification bodies; **ISO/IEC 42006:2025** sets requirements for those bodies, which strengthens confidence in certificates. Customers increasingly ask AI suppliers for 42001 certification during procurement, in the same way they ask for ISO/IEC 27001 or SOC 2 reports.

### How they fit together
- **Laws** create obligations; **ISO/IEC 42001** provides the management system to meet them; the **NIST AI RMF** strengthens the risk practices inside it.
- An **obligations register** maps each legal requirement to controls and owners.
- A **crosswalk** maps controls across frameworks, so one control (for example, “impact assessment before deployment”) produces evidence for the AI Act, GDPR DPIA requirements, NIST MAP outcomes and 42001 clause 6.1.4 at the same time.

blocks.title: Match the source to what it gives you
pairs: Binding, risk-tiered legal obligations for providers and deployers
Voluntary functions: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage
Certifiable requirements for an AI management system
Twelve generative AI risks with suggested actions
Guidance on assessing AI system impacts on people and society

blocks.title: Common distinctions
blocks.md:
- The **NIST AI RMF** is *voluntary* and *not certifiable*. **ISO/IEC 42001** is voluntary but *certifiable*.
- In the RMF, **Govern** is the cross-cutting function; **Map** comes first in the life of a system (context before measurement).
- ISO/IEC 42001 requires both an **AI risk assessment** and an **AI system impact assessment**; the first looks at risks to the organisation and its objectives, the second at consequences for individuals, groups and society.

q.q: An organisation wants to demonstrate to customers, through independent certification, that it governs AI responsibly. Which source BEST supports this goal?
o: The NIST AI RMF
ISO/IEC 42001
NIST AI 600-1
ISO/IEC 22989
q.why: ISO/IEC 42001 specifies requirements for an AI management system that accredited bodies can certify. The NIST AI RMF and its profiles are voluntary guidance without certification, and ISO/IEC 22989 is terminology.

sections.title: What makes AI governance different, and the policy stack

scenes.title: Governing something that learns
scenes.sub: How AI governance differs from IT governance, and the policies that make it real
scenes.say: Most organisations already have IT governance, security policies and change control. So why does AI need anything new? | This video explains what is genuinely different about governing AI, and how to turn principles into policies, standards and procedures.

scenes.title: IT governance and AI governance
rows: Probabilistic: outputs vary and can be wrong
Changes as data, models and the world drift
Plus bias, safety, explainability, IP and societal harm
Plus data science, legal, ethics, HR and affected people
scenes.say: Here is what changes. | Traditional software is deterministic: the same input gives the same output, and it can be fully specified and tested. AI is probabilistic: outputs vary, and some will be wrong. | Traditional systems change when someone releases new code. AI systems also change as data, models and the world drift, sometimes with no release at all. | IT risk focuses on confidentiality, integrity and availability. AI adds bias, safety, explainability, intellectual property and wider societal harm. | And AI governance needs more people at the table: data scientists, lawyers, ethicists, HR and, often, the people affected by the system.

scenes.title: What AI governance adds

items.h: An inventory of AI use cases
items.d: You can’t govern what you don’t know about

items.h: Risk and impact assessment per use case
items.d: Proportionate to the harm a use case could cause
From data sourcing to monitoring and retirement
A committee that can approve, condition or reject
Monitoring, audits and reassessment, not one-off approval

scenes.say: AI governance builds on IT governance rather than replacing it, and adds five things. | An inventory of every AI use case, because you can’t govern what you don’t know about. | Risk and impact assessment for each use case, proportionate to the harm it could cause. | Controls across the whole life cycle, from data sourcing and training through deployment, monitoring and retirement. | Cross-functional decision-making, usually a committee with the authority to approve, add conditions or reject. | And continuous oversight: monitoring, audits and reassessment, because a one-off approval doesn’t stay valid for a system that changes.

scenes.title: From intent to action

layers.label: Policy
layers.sub: Management intent. Mandatory, high-level, rarely changes

layers.label: Standards
layers.sub: Mandatory, specific requirements that make the policy measurable

layers.label: Procedures
layers.sub: Step-by-step instructions for carrying out a task

layers.label: Guidelines
layers.sub: Recommended good practice; advisory, not mandatory

scenes.say: Governance becomes real through a hierarchy of documents. | At the top, a policy states management’s intent. It is mandatory, high level, approved by senior leadership, and rarely changes. For example: AI may only be used in ways that are lawful, assessed for risk, and subject to appropriate human oversight. | Standards make the policy specific and measurable, and are also mandatory. For example: every high-risk AI system must have a completed impact assessment and pass adversarial testing before release. | Procedures are step-by-step instructions, such as how to submit a new AI use case for approval. | And guidelines are recommended good practice, such as tips for writing safe prompts. They are advisory, not mandatory.

scenes.title: A typical AI policy set

items.d: Principles, scope, roles, decision rights
Approved tools; what data may be entered
Tiers, assessments, approvals, reviews
Data, testing, deployment, monitoring
Due diligence and contract terms
Reporting, triage, containment

scenes.say: Most organisations end up with a similar set of documents. | An AI governance policy sets principles, scope, roles and decision rights. | An acceptable use policy tells staff which AI tools are approved and what data they may enter into them. | An AI risk management standard defines risk tiers, required assessments, approval routes and review frequency. | An AI lifecycle standard sets requirements for data, testing, deployment and monitoring. | A third-party AI standard covers due diligence and contract terms for AI suppliers. | And an AI incident procedure explains how to report, triage and contain AI-specific incidents.

AI governance extends IT governance; it doesn’t replace it
Policy states intent; standards make it measurable
Procedures say how; guidelines advise
scenes.say: To recap. | AI is probabilistic, it drifts, and it introduces new kinds of harm. | So AI governance extends existing IT, data, privacy and security governance, rather than replacing them. | A policy states mandatory intent, and standards make it specific and measurable. | Procedures explain how to do things, and guidelines offer advice.

blocks.md:
### Why AI needs its own governance
AI governance is not a new silo. It builds on IT governance (such as COBIT), information security management (such as ISO/IEC 27001), privacy programmes and data governance. But AI changes several assumptions those programmes rely on:

| Assumption in traditional IT | Why AI breaks it | Governance response |
|---|---|---|
| Behaviour is fully specified by code | Behaviour is learned from data and is probabilistic | Evaluate statistically; define acceptable error rates; require human oversight where errors matter |
| Systems change only through releases | Data, concept and behavioural drift change outcomes without releases | Continuous monitoring with reassessment triggers |
| Testing can cover the requirements | Inputs are open-ended; emergent and adversarial behaviour exists | Red teaming, adversarial testing, guardrails, staged rollout |
| Risk is mainly CIA | Bias, safety, explainability, IP, misinformation, societal impact | Broader risk taxonomy and impact assessments |
| Ownership sits with IT | Value and harm sit with the business and with affected people | Cross-functional decision rights; named business owners |
| Suppliers provide fixed products | Hosted models update silently; training data is opaque | Version pinning, contractual notification rights, AI-specific due diligence |

Effective AI governance is therefore **risk-based** (more scrutiny for higher-impact uses), **lifecycle-based** (controls at every stage, not just at approval), and **cross-functional** (legal, privacy, security, risk, ethics, HR and business owners share decisions).

### Policies, standards, procedures and guidelines
The classic document hierarchy applies, and ISC2 exams expect you to know it precisely:

- **Policy:** a high-level statement of management intent and direction. Mandatory. Approved by senior management or the board. Technology-neutral and stable. *Example: “The organisation will use AI only in ways that are lawful, risk-assessed, transparent to affected people and subject to appropriate human oversight.”*
- **Standard:** a mandatory, specific requirement that supports a policy and makes it measurable. *Example: “All Tier 3 AI systems must complete an impact assessment, a bias evaluation and an adversarial test before production.”*
- **Baseline:** a minimum level of configuration or control, often expressed as settings. *Example: “All AI gateways log prompts and completions for 90 days with personal data masked.”*
- **Procedure:** detailed, step-by-step instructions for performing a task consistently. *Example: “How to register a new AI use case in the inventory.”*
- **Guideline:** recommended practice that is advisory, not mandatory. *Example: “Tips for writing prompts that avoid entering personal data.”*

### What an AI acceptable use policy should cover
Generative AI made acceptable use urgent, because every employee can now use powerful AI tools in a browser. A good acceptable use policy:
1. Lists **approved tools** and explains how to request new ones.
2. Defines **data rules**: which classifications may be entered into which tools (for example, no confidential or personal data in consumer tools; approved enterprise tools may process internal data).
3. Requires **human review** of AI output before it is relied on, published or sent to customers.
4. Sets **transparency** expectations: when AI use must be disclosed to colleagues, customers or the public.
5. Prohibits specific uses, such as making employment decisions solely with AI, or generating content that impersonates real people.
6. Explains **how to report** problems, including suspected data leaks or harmful outputs.
7. States **consequences** of non-compliance and is acknowledged by staff.

Policies should be reviewed at least annually and whenever regulation, technology or the organisation’s use of AI changes significantly. Because AI moves fast, many organisations keep the policy stable and update the *standards* and *approved tool lists* more frequently.

blocks.title: Policy, standard, procedure or guideline?
pairs: “AI will be used only in lawful, risk-assessed and overseen ways.”
“High-risk AI must pass adversarial testing before release.”
“Step 1: open the intake form. Step 2: attach the impact assessment…”
“Consider rewording prompts to avoid including customer names.”

blocks.title: The policy that never changes anything
blocks.md: A bank’s board approved a well-written “Responsible AI Policy” eighteen months ago. An internal review finds that no AI system has been assessed against it, nobody knows which systems count as “high impact”, and developers say they don’t know what the policy requires them to do.

o: A longer, more detailed policy that spells out every rule for each type of AI system
Standards and procedures that define tiers, required assessments and approval steps, with owners
A new set of ethical principles agreed by the board and published alongside the existing policy
A public statement about the bank’s commitment to AI ethics, signed by the chief executive officer
q.why: Policies state intent but are not directly actionable. Standards make requirements specific and measurable, and procedures tell people exactly what to do. Without them, and without owners, the policy has no operational effect.

q.q: Which characteristic of AI systems MOST justifies continuous monitoring and reassessment rather than one-time approval?
o: AI systems are usually hosted in the cloud, where providers change the infrastructure frequently
Their behaviour can change through data, concept and model drift even without a code release
AI systems cost more to run than traditional systems, so their budgets need regular review
AI systems are approved once for a fixed purpose, so reassessment only matters when that purpose changes
q.why: Unlike deterministic software, AI outcomes change as data and the world change, and hosted models can be updated by providers. A one-time approval quickly goes stale, so governance must be continuous.

sections.title: AI use-case inventories and organisational roles

scenes.title: Who owns the AI?
scenes.sub: Use-case inventories, decision rights, and the people who make governance work
scenes.say: Two questions sink most AI governance programmes: what AI do we actually have, and who is accountable for it? | This video covers the centralised AI use-case inventory, and the roles that make governance work, from the board to the AI champion in each team.

scenes.title: The life of a use case

note.text: The inventory is a living record, not a one-time list.

scenes.say: A centralised inventory works best as part of a process. Use cases enter through intake, either as a new request, or because monitoring or procurement discovered AI already in use. | Triage decides whether it really is AI, and gives it a provisional risk tier. | The use case is assessed for risk and impact, in proportion to its tier. | A decision-maker with the right authority approves it, approves it with conditions, or rejects it. | The decision, owner, tier, controls and review dates are recorded in the inventory. | And the record is updated as the system is monitored, reviewed, changed and eventually retired.

scenes.title: What each inventory record holds

items.d: Name, description, business process, intended use
Business owner, technical owner, data owner
Model, version, vendor, hosting location
Categories used, personal or sensitive data, sources
Tier, assessments, HITL mode, controls
Lifecycle stage, approval, next review

scenes.say: Each inventory record should answer a standard set of questions. | Identity and purpose: what the system is, which business process it supports, and what it is intended to do. | Accountable owners: a named business owner, technical owner and data owner. | Models and suppliers: which model and version, from which vendor, hosted where. | Data: which categories of data it uses, including personal or sensitive data, and their sources. | Risk and oversight: the risk tier, completed assessments, the human oversight mode, and the controls in place. | And status and dates: lifecycle stage, approval date and next review date.

scenes.title: Roles that make it work

items.d: Set risk appetite; hold management to account
Owns AI strategy, governance and coordination
Cross-functional body that approves and conditions use cases
Champions responsible AI; reviews ethical impacts
Advocates in each team; first point of contact

scenes.say: Now the people. | The board and executive leadership set the organisation’s appetite for AI risk, and hold management accountable. | A chief AI officer owns AI strategy and governance, and coordinates across functions. US federal agencies, for example, are required to designate one. | An AI governance committee brings legal, privacy, security, risk, ethics, HR, data science and business leaders together to approve, condition or reject use cases. | An AI ethics officer champions responsible AI principles and reviews ethical impacts, such as fairness and effects on vulnerable groups. | And AI champions are trained advocates embedded in each team. They promote safe adoption, answer questions, and spot unregistered AI early.

scenes.title: Three lines for AI
rows: Business owners, AI and data teams
Own and manage the risk day to day
scenes.say: Many organisations map these roles onto the three lines model. | The first line is the business owners and the AI and data teams who build and run systems. The second line is risk, compliance, security and privacy. The third line is internal audit. | The first line owns and manages AI risk day to day. The second sets frameworks and provides challenge and oversight. And the third gives the board independent assurance that the whole system works.

items: A central inventory: discover, triage, assess, decide, record
Every record has named owners, a tier and review dates
CAIO, governance committee, ethics officer, champions
First line owns risk; second oversees; third assures
scenes.say: To recap. | A centralised inventory sits inside a process: discover, triage, assess, decide and record. | Every record has named owners, a risk tier, its controls and review dates. | Key roles include the chief AI officer, a cross-functional governance committee, an AI ethics officer and AI champions. | And in the three lines model, the first line owns AI risk, the second oversees it, and the third provides independent assurance.

blocks.md:
### Why a centralised inventory matters
An organisation cannot assess, monitor, audit or report on AI it does not know about. A **centralised AI use-case inventory** (sometimes called an AI register or AI system catalogue) is the foundation of every other governance activity:

- **Risk management:** tiers, assessments and controls are tracked per use case.
- **Compliance:** the EU AI Act requires providers and certain deployers of high-risk systems to register them in an EU database; US federal agencies must publish annual AI use-case inventories; ISO/IEC 42001 auditors expect to see one.
- **Incident response:** when a model vulnerability or vendor breach is announced, the inventory tells you within minutes which systems are affected.
- **Strategy and cost:** duplicate tools, unused licences and high-value opportunities become visible.

### Building and maintaining it
- **Define “AI” for inventory purposes.** Include machine learning models, generative AI tools and features embedded in SaaS products, and agents. Exclude simple rules engines unless policy says otherwise. Ambiguity is the main reason inventories are incomplete.
- **Use multiple discovery channels.** Self-registration through intake; procurement and contract reviews; expense claims; network, proxy and cloud-access logs; SaaS management tools; code repositories and model registries; and questions in annual attestations. Shadow AI detection is covered in Module 2.6.
- **Integrate with existing records.** Link inventory entries to the CMDB, data catalogue, vendor register, model registry and risk register rather than duplicating them.
- **Keep it alive.** Require updates on material change (new model version, new data, new users or purpose), schedule reviews by tier, and record retirement.

A useful test: *if a regulator, auditor or journalist asked tomorrow which of our systems make decisions about people, could we answer accurately within a day?*

### Organisational roles
| Role | Typical responsibilities |
|---|---|
| **Board** | Approves AI strategy and risk appetite; receives assurance; holds management to account |
| **Chief AI Officer (CAIO)** | Owns AI strategy and the governance programme; coordinates across functions; reports on AI risk and value. Required for US federal agencies under OMB policy |
| **AI governance committee** (council or board) | Cross-functional body (legal, privacy, security, risk, compliance, HR, data science, business) that approves, conditions or rejects higher-risk use cases and resolves escalations |
| **AI ethics officer** | Champions responsible AI principles; leads ethical reviews, fairness assessments and stakeholder engagement; can escalate concerns independently |
| **AI champions** | Trained advocates in business units; promote safe adoption, answer first-line questions, encourage registration of use cases, feed back practical issues |
| **Business (use-case) owner** | Accountable for the use case, its outcomes, its risks and its compliance |
| **Model owner / technical owner** | Responsible for the model’s development, performance, documentation and monitoring |
| **Data owner and data steward** | Accountable for data quality, classification, permitted use and access decisions |
| **CISO and security team** | AI threat modelling, security testing, monitoring and incident response |
| **Data protection officer** | Advises on GDPR compliance, DPIAs and data subject rights; independent by law where required |
| **Internal audit** | Independent assurance over AI governance and controls |

Two principles underpin this structure. **Accountability must be named:** every AI system needs a single accountable business owner, not “the AI team”. And **decision rights must match risk:** low-risk uses can be approved by a manager using a checklist, while high-impact uses go to the committee, and some decisions (such as accepting significant residual risk) require an executive.

blocks.title: Decision rights by tier (example)
items: Tier 1: low
Example: an AI writing assistant with no personal data. **Assessment:** short checklist. **Approver:** line manager plus AI champion. **Review:** annually.
Tier 2: moderate

Example: an internal knowledge assistant using company documents. **Assessment:** standard risk assessment and security review. **Approver:** business owner with security and privacy sign-off. **Review:** every six months and on material change.
Tier 3: high

Example: AI that screens job applicants or influences credit decisions. **Assessment:** full risk and impact assessment, DPIA, bias testing, adversarial testing. **Approver:** AI governance committee; residual risk accepted by an executive. **Review:** quarterly, with continuous monitoring.
Prohibited
Example: emotion recognition to evaluate employees. **Decision:** not permitted under policy (and, in the EU, under law). Requests are recorded and declined.

blocks.title: Accountability questions
blocks.md: Exam scenarios often ask **who** should decide or **who is accountable**. The answer is rarely the data scientist or the AI tool itself. Look for the **business owner** (accountable for the use case), the **governance committee** (approval of high-risk uses), or **senior management** (accepting significant residual risk). Security teams advise and implement controls; they don’t usually *own* business risk.

q.q: A critical vulnerability is announced in a popular open-source model. Which governance capability MOST directly lets the organisation identify every affected system quickly?
o: An AI ethics statement that commits every team to report vulnerabilities promptly
A centralised AI use-case inventory that records models, versions, owners and uses
A guideline on prompt writing that tells staff which models are approved for use
An annual awareness campaign that reminds developers to track the open-source components they use
q.why: An inventory that records which models and versions each system uses, and who owns it, turns an announcement into a targeted response in minutes. The other options don’t provide that visibility.

quiz.q: Which of these is a prohibited practice under the EU AI Act?
o: A customer-service chatbot that clearly discloses to users that it is an AI system
Social scoring that leads to detrimental treatment of people
Credit scoring of loan applicants based on their financial history
An email spam filter that uses machine learning
quiz.why: Social scoring leading to detrimental or unjustified treatment is banned under Article 5. Credit scoring is high risk, a disclosed chatbot is limited risk, and spam filters are minimal risk.

quiz.q: In the NIST AI RMF, which function is cross-cutting and informs all the others?
o: Map
Measure
Manage
Govern
quiz.why: Govern establishes culture, policies, roles and accountability, and runs through Map, Measure and Manage.

quiz.q: What MOST distinguishes ISO/IEC 42001 from the NIST AI RMF?
o: ISO/IEC 42001 is an EU law with fines, while the NIST AI RMF is a US federal regulation
ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable management system standard; the NIST AI RMF is voluntary, uncertified guidance
The NIST AI RMF applies only to US federal agencies, while ISO/IEC 42001 applies to every organisation
ISO/IEC 42001 only covers generative AI, while the NIST AI RMF covers every other kind of AI system
quiz.why: Both are voluntary, but 42001 sets auditable requirements for an AI management system that accredited bodies certify. The RMF is flexible guidance for any organisation.

quiz.q: An EU employer uses a vendor’s AI tool to rank job applicants. Under the EU AI Act, the employer is MOST likely:
o: The provider of a minimal-risk system
The deployer of a high-risk system
Outside the scope of the Act
A general-purpose AI model provider
quiz.why: Employment and recruitment uses are listed in Annex III as high risk, and an organisation using such a system under its authority is a deployer, with its own obligations.

quiz.q: Which characteristic MOST distinguishes AI governance from traditional IT governance?
o: AI systems always cost more than traditional systems, so they need tighter budget control
AI behaviour is learned and probabilistic, and it can change through drift without a code release
AI systems rarely process personal data, so privacy governance plays a smaller role than in IT
AI systems are retrained automatically, so they never need formal change management
quiz.why: Learned, probabilistic behaviour and drift break the assumption that tested, released code behaves predictably, which drives continuous monitoring and reassessment.

quiz.q: Which document type sets mandatory, specific and measurable requirements that support a policy?
o: Guideline
Standard
Procedure
Charter
quiz.why: Standards are mandatory and specific. Policies state intent, procedures give steps, and guidelines are advisory.

quiz.q: “Consider removing customer names before pasting text into an AI tool.” What kind of document statement is this?
o: A policy
A standard
A guideline
A baseline
quiz.why: The word “consider” signals advice. Guidelines recommend good practice but are not mandatory.

quiz.q: What is the PRIMARY purpose of a centralised AI use-case inventory?
o: To showcase the organisation’s AI capabilities to customers, investors and regulators
To give visibility of every AI system, its owner, risk tier and controls, so it can be governed
To replace individual risk assessments with a single register of all approved AI systems
To store every model’s weights and training data securely in one central, access-controlled location
quiz.why: Every other governance activity depends on knowing what AI exists, who owns it and how risky it is.

quiz.q: Who should be accountable for an AI use case’s outcomes and risks?
o: The vendor that supplied the model
A named business owner
The most senior data scientist
The AI tool itself
quiz.why: Accountability belongs to a named business owner who benefits from the use case and can make decisions about it. Technical teams and vendors have responsibilities, but not ownership of the business risk.

quiz.q: What is the MAIN role of AI champions?
o: To approve all high-risk AI use cases on behalf of the governance committee
To act as trained advocates in their teams and a first point of contact for safe AI use
To conduct independent audits of AI systems and report findings directly to the board
To replace the chief AI officer in business units that don’t have their own AI leadership
quiz.why: Champions extend the governance programme into business units. Approval of high-risk uses sits with the committee, and independent assurance with internal audit.

exam.q: A US software company with no EU offices sells an AI hiring tool to employers in the EU. Which statement is MOST accurate?
o: The EU AI Act doesn’t apply, because the company has no establishment anywhere in the EU
As a provider placing a high-risk system on the EU market, the company must meet provider obligations
Only the GDPR applies, because the tool processes candidates’ personal data rather than products
Only the EU employers have obligations under the Act, because they are the ones using the tool
exam.why: The AI Act applies to providers placing systems on the EU market regardless of where they are established. Hiring tools are high risk, so provider duties such as risk management, documentation and conformity assessment apply. Deployers have separate duties.

exam.q: A multinational must meet EU AI Act duties, GDPR requirements and customer demands for assurance. Which approach is MOST efficient and defensible?
o: Run a separate compliance programme for each requirement, so each has a dedicated owner and budget
One AI management system with an obligations register and crosswalks, so shared controls evidence everything
Adopt the NIST AI RMF across the group, since a recognised framework satisfies the EU AI Act and GDPR
Meet the strictest requirement in each area and assume that this automatically satisfies all the others
exam.why: A single management system, for example aligned to ISO/IEC 42001, with obligations mapped to shared controls, avoids duplication and produces consistent evidence. Frameworks never override legal obligations.

exam.q: A CIO proposes governing AI solely through the existing change advisory board, which reviews releases before deployment. What is the MOST significant gap?
o: Change boards are too slow for AI, so AI releases should bypass them and go through the data science team
Release review misses drift, impact on people, bias, legal review and monitoring after deployment
Change boards can’t review cloud-hosted systems, so any hosted model would fall outside their remit
AI systems rarely change after deployment, so a change board would have too little to review
exam.why: AI outcomes can change without releases and raise harms beyond CIA. Governance needs risk and impact assessment, cross-functional decisions and ongoing monitoring in addition to change control.

exam.q: Employees are pasting customer records into consumer AI chatbots, despite a high-level responsible AI policy. Which action is MOST effective?
o: Re-issue the existing policy with stronger wording and a reminder of the disciplinary consequences
Provide an approved enterprise tool, an acceptable-use standard by data class, training and technical controls
Block all AI websites on the corporate network and ban AI use permanently until further notice
Ask every employee to re-read and sign the policy, and have managers audit a sample of signatures each quarter
exam.why: Policies need actionable standards, a sanctioned alternative and enforcement. Banning AI typically drives use underground, and re-issuing the same policy changes nothing.

exam.q: Internal audit finds the AI inventory lists 40 systems, but SaaS discovery tools show 130 AI-enabled applications in use. What is the BEST next step?
o: Block all 90 unregistered applications immediately until each one has been fully assessed
Triage them into the inventory through risk-based intake, assign owners and tiers, and fix the intake gaps
Redefine “AI” in the policy to exclude AI features embedded in SaaS products, which vendors manage
Ask each vendor to confirm in writing that its AI features are safe and compliant, and record each confirmation
exam.why: A risk-based triage brings unknown AI under governance proportionately. Blanket blocking disrupts the business and drives shadow use, and vendors don’t carry the organisation’s accountability.

exam.q: A high-impact AI credit model has residual risk above the team’s authority after all planned controls. Who should decide whether to accept it?
o: The lead data scientist, who understands the model and its limitations best
The CISO, because AI risk is ultimately a technology and information security risk that the CISO owns
A senior executive with authority under the risk appetite, advised by the governance committee
The model vendor, which is accountable for the risks of the product it supplies
exam.why: Residual risk must be accepted by someone with authority matching its level, usually a senior business executive acting within board-approved risk appetite. Technical leads and the CISO advise but don’t own business risk.
